questions.question_text: Why is the interval $0\le x\le 2\pi$ NOT a suitable restricted domain for defining an inverse of $y=\cos x$?

options.text: The line $y=0$ cuts the curve twice on this interval, so $\cos x$ is not one-to-one.
$\cos x$ is undefined at $x=\pi$, so the function is not defined on the whole interval.
options.why: Cosine is defined for every real number; $\cos\pi=-1$.

options.text: The curve takes only positive values on this interval, so it misses the negative values in its range.
options.why: On $0\le x\le 2\pi$, $\cos x$ reaches from $-1$ up to $1$, so it covers the entire range.

options.text: A vertical line cuts the curve more than once, so the graph is not a function.
options.why: Confuses the vertical line test with the horizontal line test; $y=\cos x$ is already a function.

questions.solution_text:
2. **Check no horizontal line meets the curve more than once on the interval**
$\cos\frac{\pi}{2}=0$ and $\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}=0$, and both values lie in $0\le x\le 2\pi$.
The horizontal line $y=0$ cuts the curve twice, so $y=\cos x$ fails the horizontal line test on this interval.

questions.question_text: Which interval is the agreed restricted domain used to define the inverse of $y=\cos x$?

options.why: Kept a whole period, but $\cos\frac{\pi}{3}=\cos\frac{5\pi}{3}$, so this piece is not one-to-one.
Quoted the sine restriction; cosine is even, so $\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=\cos\frac{\pi}{3}$ and this piece is not one-to-one.
Chose a symmetric interval, but cosine is even so every non-zero $x$ pairs with $-x$ at the same height.

questions.solution_text:
On $0\le x\le\pi$ the cosine curve falls steadily from $\cos 0=1$ to $\cos\pi=-1$.
No horizontal line cuts this piece twice, and it takes every value in $[-1,1]$.
$0\le x\le\pi$

questions.question_text: Which statement best explains why the domain of $y=\sin x$ must be restricted before an inverse function can be defined?

options.text: A horizontal line can cut $y=\sin x$ more than once, so the function is not one-to-one and its inverse relation is not a function.
A vertical line can cut $y=\sin x$ more than once, so $y=\sin x$ is not a function.
options.why: Confuses the vertical line test with the horizontal one; $y=\sin x$ passes the vertical line test and is a function.

options.text: The range of $y=\sin x$ is only $[-1,1]$, so the inverse relation has too small a domain.
options.why: A small domain is not a problem; the restricted sine has the same range and does have an inverse function.

options.text: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is unbounded to the left and right, so the inverse relation has no vertical asymptotes.
options.why: Names the domain of $y=\sin x$ rather than the repetition of $y$-values, which is the actual obstacle.

questions.solution_text:
An inverse function must send each output back to exactly one input.
The line $y=\frac{1}{2}$ meets $y=\sin x$ infinitely often, so one output comes from many inputs.
The curve therefore fails the horizontal line test, and the domain must be restricted before an inverse function exists.

questions.question_text: For $f(x)=\tan x$, which is the largest interval containing $x=\pi$ on which the function is defined everywhere and has an inverse function?

options.why: Included the asymptotes at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$, where tangent is undefined.
Selected the principal branch, which does not contain $x=\pi$.
Included the undefined point $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and the repeated value $\tan0=\tan\pi=0$.

questions.solution_text:
The branch containing $x=\pi$ lies between the asymptotes at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$.
Tangent increases steadily on this branch, so it is one-to-one.
The endpoints are excluded because tangent is undefined there.
The largest interval is $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$.

questions.question_text: Which interval could be used as a restricted domain for $y=\sin x$, so that the piece is one-to-one and still takes every value from $-1$ to $1$?

options.why: Not one-to-one: $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{1}{2}$, and both lie in the interval.
One-to-one, but it only reaches from $-1$ up to $0$, so it misses every positive value.
Not one-to-one: a whole period repeats every value of $\sin x$ except $\pm 1$.

questions.solution_text:
On $\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{3\pi}{2}$ the sine curve falls steadily from $\sin\frac{\pi}{2}=1$ to $\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=-1$.
A steadily falling piece is one-to-one, and running from $1$ down to $-1$ it takes every value in $[-1,1]$.
$\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{3\pi}{2}$

options.why: Quoted the standard cosine restriction instead of reading the thick section off the graph.
Read the matching rising piece on the left of the origin rather than the one that is drawn thick.
Took the endpoints from where the curve crosses the $x$-axis rather than where the thick section starts and stops.

questions.solution_text:
The thick section begins at the minimum point where $x=\pi$ and $y=-1$.
It ends at the maximum point where $x=2\pi$ and $y=1$.
$\pi\le x\le 2\pi$

questions.question_text:
The restricted domain of $y=\tan x$ is written with round brackets rather than square brackets.
Which statement gives the reason?

options.text: $\tan x$ is undefined at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, so those endpoints cannot belong to the domain.
$\tan x$ equals $0$ at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, so including the endpoints would repeat a value.
options.why: States a false value; $\tan x$ is not $0$ at $\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$, it is undefined there.

options.text: $\tan x$ has period $\pi$, so an interval of length $\pi$ must exclude one endpoint.
options.why: Uses periodicity without checking where tangent is defined; both endpoints here are excluded because tangent is undefined at each one.

options.text: $\tan x$ is an odd function, so its restricted domain must be symmetric and open about the origin.
options.why: Oddness does not require a restricted domain to be symmetric or open; the endpoints are excluded because tangent is undefined there.

questions.solution_text:
The graph of $y=\tan x$ has vertical asymptotes at $x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
There is no value of $\tan x$ at those two points, so they cannot be part of any domain.
Round brackets record that both endpoints are excluded.

questions.question_text: For $f(x)=\cos x$ on $0\le x\le4\pi$, which is the largest interval containing $x=\frac{7\pi}{2}$ on which the inverse function exists?

options.why: Kept a whole period, so $\cos\frac{5\pi}{2}=\cos\frac{7\pi}{2}=0$ and the function is not one-to-one.
Stopped at the specified input rather than the preceding turning point; the interval can extend to $3\pi$ while remaining one-to-one.
Selected the neighbouring decreasing branch, which does not contain $x=\frac{7\pi}{2}$.

questions.solution_text:
The point $x=\frac{7\pi}{2}$ lies between the turning points at $x=3\pi$ and $x=4\pi$.
On $3\pi\le x\le4\pi$, cosine increases steadily from $-1$ to $1$, so it is one-to-one.
Extending left of $3\pi$ repeats values, and $4\pi$ is the endpoint of the supplied domain.
The largest interval is $[3\pi,4\pi]$.
